neighbours.label: the sentence-final period in encyclopedic descriptive prose (strongest after a clause joined by a semicolon)
fire: The beak is short and black; the legs are bright orange. Juveniles are paler
The village has an inn; the parish church is a modest building. A fair is held yearly
He wrote poems and essays; he died in Rome at the age of 54. His letters survive
The shrub flowers in spring; the berries ripen to deep purple. It tolerates shade
The fortress was rebuilt in 1610; the walls are of local granite. Little else remains
The species feeds on insects; it roosts in hollow trees. It is rarely seen by day
The novel sold poorly at first; it was reprinted twice after his death. Critics now praise it
The river rises in the hills; its course is short and steep. Trout are common
quiet: The beak is short and black, the legs are bright orange, and juveniles are paler
The village has an inn, the parish church is a modest building, and a fair is held yearly
He wrote poems and essays, died in Rome at the age of 54, and his letters survive
The shrub flowers in spring, the berries ripen to deep purple, and it tolerates shade
The fortress was rebuilt in 1610 with walls of local granite, and little else remains
The species feeds on insects, roosts in hollow trees, and is rarely seen by day
The novel sold poorly at first, was reprinted twice after his death, and critics now praise it
The river rises in the hills with a short and steep course, and trout are common

notes: Near misses keep the text but drop the full stop (clauses joined by commas, no sentence-final period). Probing showed the semicolon helps but is not required.
